findings.summary: Microsoft began .NET Framework development in the late 1990s as NGWS, releasing version 1.0 in February 2002 to replace legacy Windows platforms. Since then, nine major upgrades have shipped, seven coinciding with new Visual Studio releases. Versions 2.0 and 4.0 introduced significant CLR updates for performance, security, and language interoperability. When the CLR version stays the same, newer framework releases typically supersede prior ones via in-place updates. The family includes .NET Compact Framework for mobile/embedded Windows CE and .NET Micro Framework for severely resource-constrained devices. .NET Framework 4.8 was announced as the last major version, with future work shifting to the cross-platform .NET Core (later simply .NET), though 4.8.1 followed in August 2022.

mechanisms.title: CLR versioning and in-place supersession
mechanisms.explanation: When the Common Language Runtime version remains unchanged, newer .NET Framework releases typically replace previous versions through in-place updates rather than side-by-side installation.

mechanisms.title: Platform-specific framework variants
mechanisms.explanation: The .NET Framework family includes reduced-footprint variants: .NET Compact Framework for Windows CE/mobile devices and .NET Micro Framework for severely resource-constrained embedded targets.
